      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Viral <span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your liver. This swelling and damage can affect how well your liver functions.</p><p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> can be an acute (short-term) infection or a <span class="qt1">chronic</span> (long-term) infection. Some types of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> cause only acute infections. Other types can cause both acute and <span class="qt1">chronic</span> infections.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p>There are different types of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>, with different causes:</p><ul><li>Viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> is the most common type. It is caused by one of several viruses -- <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> viruses A, B, C, D, and E. In the United States, A, B, and C are the most common.</li><li>Alcoholic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> is caused by heavy alcohol use</li><li>Toxic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> can be caused by certain poisons, chemicals, medicines, or supplements</li><li>Autoimmune <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> is a <span class="qt1">chronic</span> type in which your body's immune system attacks your liver. The cause is not known, but genetics and your environment may play a role.</li></ul>How is viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> spread?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis A and hepatitis</span> E usually spread through contact with food or water that was contaminated with an infected person's stool. You can also get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> E by eating undercooked pork, deer, or shellfish.</p><p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, and <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> D spread through contact with the blood of someone who has the disease. <span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B and D may also spread through contact with other body fluids. This can happen in many ways, such as sharing drug needles or having unprotected sex.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p>The risks are different for the different types of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. For example, with most of the viral types, your risk is higher if you have unprotected sex.  People who drink a lot over long periods of time are at risk for alcoholic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p>Some people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> do not have symptoms and do not know they are infected. If you do have symptoms, they may include:</p><ul><li>Fever</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Dark urine</li><li>Clay-colored bowel movements</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Jaundice, yellowing of your skin and eyes</li></ul><p>If you have an acute infection, your symptoms can start anywhere between 2 weeks to 6 months after you got infected. If you have a <span class="qt1">chronic</span> infection, you may not have symptoms until many years later.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> cause?<p><span class="qt1">Chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> can lead to complications such as cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver failure, and liver cancer. Early diagnosis and treatment of <span class="qt1">chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> may prevent these complications.</p>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>, your health care provider:</p><ul><li>Will ask about your symptoms and medical history</li><li>Will do a physical exam</li><li>Will likely do blood tests, including tests for viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span></li><li>Might do imaging tests, such as an ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI</li><li>May need to do a liver biopsy to get a clear diagnosis and check for liver damage</li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> depends on which type you have and whether it is acute or <span class="qt1">chronic</span>. Acute viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> often goes away on its own. To feel better, you may just need to rest and get enough fluids. But in some cases, it may be more serious. You might even need treatment in a hospital.</p><p>There are different medicines to treat the different <span class="qt1">chronic</span> types of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. Possible other treatments may include surgery and other medical procedures. People who have alcoholic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> need to stop drinking. If your <span class="qt1">chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> leads to liver failure or liver cancer, you may need a liver transplant.</p>Can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> be prevented?<p>There are different ways to prevent or lower your risk for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>, depending on the type of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. For example, not drinking too much alcohol can prevent alcoholic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. There are vaccines to prevent <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> A and B. Autoimmune <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> cannot be prevented.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HBV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. It can damage your liver. This swelling and damage can affect how well your liver functions.</p>What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B is a type of viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. It can cause an acute (short-term) or <span class="qt1">chronic</span> (long-term) infection. People with an acute infection usually get better on their own without treatment. Some people with <span class="qt1">chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B will need treatment.</p><p>Thanks to a vaccine, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B is not very common in the United States. It is more common in certain parts of the world, such as sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.</p>What causes <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> B is caused by the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B virus. The virus spreads through contact with blood, semen, or other body fluids from a person who has the virus.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p>Anyone can get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, but the risk is higher in:</p><ul><li>Infants born to mothers who have <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B</li><li>People who inject drugs or share needles, syringes, and other types of drug equipment</li><li>Sex partners of people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, especially if they are not using latex or polyurethane condoms during sex</li><li>Men who have sex with men</li><li>People who live with someone who has <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, especially if they use the same razor, toothbrush, or nail clippers</li><li>Health care and public-safety workers who are exposed to blood on the job</li><li>Hemodialysis patients</li><li>People who have lived in or traveled often to parts of the world where <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B is common</li><li>People who have diabetes, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, or HIV</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p>Often, people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B don't have symptoms. Adults and children over 5 are more likely to have symptoms than younger children.</p><p>Some people with acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B have symptoms 2 to 5 months after infection. These symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Diarrhea</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Yellowish eyes and skin, called jaundice</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt1">chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, you may not have symptoms until complications develop. This could be decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B screening is important, even if you have no symptoms. Screening means that you are tested for a disease even though you don't have symptoms. If you are at high risk, your health care provider may suggest  screening.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B cause?<p>In rare cases, acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B can cause liver failure.</p><p><span class="qt1">Chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B can develop into a serious disease that causes long-term health problems such as cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver cancer, and liver failure.</p><p>If you have ever had <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, the virus may become active again, or reactivated, later in life. This could start to damage the liver and cause symptoms.</p>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, your health care provider may use many tools to make a diagnosis:</p><ul><li>A medical history, which includes asking about your symptoms</li><li>A physical exam</li><li>Blood tests, including tests for viral <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span></li></ul>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B?<p>If you have acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B, you probably don't need treatment. Some people with <span class="qt1">chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B don't need treatment. But if you have a <span class="qt1">chronic</span> infection and blood tests show that <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B could be damaging your liver, you may need to take antiviral medicines.</p>Can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B be prevented?<p>The best way to prevent <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B is to get the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B vaccine.</p><p>You can also reduce your chance of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B infection by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools</li><li>Not sharing personal items, such as toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>If you think you have been in contact with the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B virus, see your health care provider right away. Your provider may give you a dose of the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B vaccine to prevent infection. In some cases, your provider may also give you a medicine called <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> B immune globulin (HBIG). You need to get the vaccine and the HBIG (if needed) as soon as possible after coming into contact with the virus. It is best if you can get them within 24 hours.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/hepatitisc.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">HCV</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver. Inflammation</span> is swelling that happens when tissues of the body are injured or infected. Inflammation can damage organs.</p><p>There are different types of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. One type, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, is caused by the <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C virus (HCV). <span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C can range from a mild illness lasting a few weeks to a serious, lifelong illness.</p><p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C can be acute or <span class="qt1">chronic</span>:</p><ul><li>Acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C is a short-term infection. The symptoms can last up to 6 months. Sometimes your body is able to fight off the infection and the virus goes away. But for most people, an acute infection leads to <span class="qt1">chronic</span> infection.</li><li><span class="qt1">Chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C is a long-lasting infection. If it is not treated, it can last for a lifetime and cause serious health problems, including liver damage, cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), liver cancer, and even death.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C spread?<p><span class="qt0">Hepatitis</span> C spreads through contact with the blood of someone who has HCV. This contact may be through:</p><ul><li>Sharing drug needles or other drug materials with someone who has HCV. In the United States, this is the most common way that people get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C.</li><li>Getting an accidental stick with a needle that was used on someone who has HCV. This can happen in health care settings.</li><li>Being tattooed or pierced with tools or inks that were not sterilized after being used on someone who has HCV.</li><li>Having contact with the blood or open sores of someone who has HCV.</li><li>Sharing personal care items that may have come in contact with another person's blood, such as razors or toothbrushes.</li><li>Being born to a mother with HCV.</li><li>Having unprotected sex with someone who has HCV.</li></ul><p>Before 1992, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C was also commonly spread through blood transfusions and organ transplants. Since then, there has been routine testing of the U.S. blood supply for HCV. It is now very rare for someone to get HCV this way.</p>Who is more likely to get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p>You are more likely to get <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C if you:</p><ul><li>Have injected drugs</li><li>Had a blood transfusion or organ transplant before July 1992</li><li>Have hemophilia and received clotting factor before 1987</li><li>Have been on kidney dialysis</li><li>Have been in contact with blood or infected needles at work</li><li>Have had tattoos or body piercings</li><li>Have worked or lived in a prison</li><li>Were born to a mother with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C</li><li>Have HIV</li><li>Have had more than one sex partner in the last 6 months</li><li>Have had a sexually transmitted infection (STI)</li><li>Are a man who has had sex with men (MSM)</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, your health care provider will likely recommend that you get tested for it.</p>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p>Most people with <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C have no symptoms. Some people with acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C do have symptoms within 1 to 3 months after they are exposed to the virus. These symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Dark yellow urine</li><li>Fatigue</li><li>Fever</li><li>Gray- or clay-colored stools</li><li>Joint pain</li><li>Loss of appetite</li><li>Nausea and/or vomiting</li><li>Pain in your abdomen (belly)</li><li>Jaundice (yellowish eyes and skin)</li></ul><p>If you have <span class="qt1">chronic</span> <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, you probably will not have symptoms until it causes complications. This can happen decades after you were infected. For this reason, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C screening is important, even if you have no symptoms.</p>What other problems can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C cause?<p>Without treatment, <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C may lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, and liver cancer. Early diagnosis and treatment of <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C can prevent these complications.</p>How is <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C diagnosed?<p>Providers diagnose <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C based on your medical history, a physical exam, and blood tests.</p><p>If you do have <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, you may need additional tests to check for liver damage. These tests may include other blood tests, an ultrasound of the liver, and a liver biopsy.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C?<p>Treatment for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C is with antiviral medicines. They can cure the disease in most cases.</p><p>If you have acute <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C, your provider may wait to see if your infection becomes <span class="qt1">chronic</span> before starting treatment.</p><p>If your <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C causes cirrhosis, you should see a doctor who specializes in liver diseases. Treatments for health problems related to cirrhosis include medicines, surgery, and other medical procedures. If your <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C leads to liver failure or liver cancer, you may need a liver transplant.</p>Can <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C be prevented?<p>There is no vaccine for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C. But you can help protect yourself from <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C infection by:</p><ul><li>Not sharing drug needles or other drug materials.</li><li>Wearing gloves if you have to touch another person's blood or open sores.</li><li>Making sure your tattoo artist or body piercer uses sterile tools and unopened ink.</li><li>Not sharing personal items such toothbrushes, razors, or nail clippers.</li><li>Using a latex condom during sex. If your or your partner is allergic to latex, you can use polyurethane condoms.</li></ul><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/cirrhosis.html">
      <content name="title">Cirrhosis</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Liver Cirrhosis</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hepatic fibrosis</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Cirrhosis is scarring of the liver. Scar tissue forms because of injury or long-term disease. Scar tissue cannot do what healthy liver tissue does - make protein, help fight infections, clean the blood, help digest food and store energy.   Cirrhosis can lead to  :</p><ul><li>Easy bruising or bleeding, or nosebleeds</li><li>Swelling of the abdomen or legs </li><li>Extra sensitivity to medicines</li><li>High blood pressure in the vein entering the liver</li><li>Enlarged veins called varices in the esophagus and stomach. Varices can bleed suddenly.</li><li> Kidney failure</li><li>Jaundice</li><li>Severe itching</li><li>Gallstones</li></ul><p>A small number of people with cirrhosis get liver cancer.</p><p>Your doctor will diagnose cirrhosis with blood tests, imaging tests, or a biopsy.</p><p>Cirrhosis has many causes. In the United States, the most common causes are <span class="qt1">chronic</span> alcoholism and <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span>. Nothing will make the scar tissue disappear, but treating the cause can keep it from getting worse. If too much scar tissue forms, you may need to consider a liver transplant.  </p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/steatoticliverdisease.html">
      <content name="title">Steatotic Liver Disease</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Fatty Liver Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">ALD</content>
      <content name="altTitle">MASLD</content>
      <content name="altTitle">NAFLD</content>
      <content name="altTitle">SLD</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is steatotic liver disease?<p>Your liver is the largest organ inside your body. It helps you digest food, store energy, and remove harmful substances (toxins). Steatotic liver disease, formerly called fatty liver disease, happens when too much fat builds up in your liver. It's typical to have some fat in your liver cells, but too much can be a problem.</p><p>There are two main types of steatotic liver disease:</p><ul><li>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)</li><li>Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD)</li></ul>What is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD)?<p>MASLD is a type of steatotic liver disease that is not caused by heavy alcohol use. It used to be called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. There are two main forms:</p><ul><li>Simple fatty liver, in which you have fat in your liver but little or no <span class="qt0">inflammation or liver</span> damage. This form usually does not get bad enough to cause liver damage or complications.</li><li>Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis, or MASH (previously called nonalcoholic steatohepatitis or NASH), is when MASLD gets worse. In addition to fat in your liver, MASH may cause <span class="qt0">inflammation and liver</span> damage. This can lead to fibrosis, or scarring, of the liver. This scarring sometimes leads to cirrhosis or liver cancer.</li></ul>What is alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD)?<p>ALD is caused by heavy alcohol use. It used to be called alcoholic fatty liver disease, or alcoholic steatohepatitis.</p><p>Your liver breaks down most of the alcohol you drink, so it can be removed from your body. But the process of breaking it down can create harmful substances. These substances can damage liver cells, cause inflammation, and weaken your body's natural defenses. The more alcohol that you drink, the more you damage your liver.  ALD is the earliest stage of alcohol-related liver disease. The next stages are alcoholic <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> and cirrhosis.</p>Who is more likely to develop steatotic liver disease?<p>The cause of MASLD is unknown, but it is more common in people who:</p><ul><li>Have type 2 diabetes and prediabetes</li><li>Have obesity</li><li>Are middle aged or older (although children can also get it)</li><li>Have high cholesterol or triglycerides</li><li>Have high blood pressure</li><li>Take certain medicines, such as corticosteroids and some cancer medicines</li><li>Have certain metabolic disorders, including metabolic syndrome</li><li>Have rapid weight loss</li><li>Have certain infections, such as <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> C</li><li>Have been exposed to certain harmful substances</li></ul><p>MASLD is the most common <span class="qt1">chronic</span> (long-term) liver disease due to increasing rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and high cholesterol.</p><p>ALD only happens in people who are heavy drinkers, especially those who have been drinking for a long period of time. The risk is higher for people who drink heavily and are women, have obesity, or have certain gene changes (known as variants or mutations).</p>What are the symptoms of steatotic liver disease?<p>Both MASLD and ALD usually have few or no symptoms. If you do have symptoms, you may feel tired or have discomfort in the upper right side of your abdomen (belly).</p>How is steatotic liver disease diagnosed?<p>Because there are often no symptoms, it's not easy to find steatotic liver disease. Your health care provider may suspect you have it if you have abnormal results on liver tests. To make a diagnosis, your provider may use:</p><ul><li>Your medical history.  This may include asking about your alcohol use and any medicines you take.</li><li>A physical exam. This may include checking your height and weight. Your provider may also check your body for signs of liver disease such as an enlarged liver or jaundice, a condition that causes your skin and whites of your eyes to turn yellow.</li><li>Blood tests. These may include liver function tests and blood count tests.</li><li>Imaging tests. These tests may be used to check for fat in the liver and for fibrosis.</li>
<li>A biopsy. In some cases, a biopsy may be done to confirm the diagnosis and check for liver damage.</li></ul>What are the treatments for steatotic liver disease?<p>The first step in treating MASLD is usually weight loss. Losing weight can reduce fat in the <span class="qt0">liver, inflammation</span>, and fibrosis. If your provider thinks that a certain medicine is the cause of your MASLD, they may tell you to stop or switch medicines. But don't stop taking any medicines unless your provider tells you to.</p><p>More studies are needed to see whether certain medicines are safe and effective to treat MASLD. Currently, no medicines are approved for treatment.</p><p>The most important part of treating ALD is to stop drinking alcohol. If you need help, you may benefit from counseling, a recovery program, or medicines that reduce cravings or make you feel sick if you drink alcohol.</p><p>Both ALD and one type of MASLD can lead to cirrhosis. Health problems caused by cirrhosis may be treated with medicines, surgery, and other medical procedures. If cirrhosis leads to liver failure, you may need a liver transplant.</p>What are some lifestyle changes that can help with steatotic liver disease?<p>If you have any type of steatotic liver disease, there are some lifestyle changes that can help:</p><ul><li>Eat a healthy diet, limiting salt and sugar, plus eating lots of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.</li><li>Talk with your provider about vaccinations. If you have <span class="qt1">chronic</span> liver disease you are more likely to get infections. Your provider may recommend vaccinations for <span class="qt0">hepatitis</span> A and B, the flu and pneumococcal disease.</li><li>Get regular exercise, which can help you lose weight and reduce fat in the liver.</li></ul><p>Check with your provider before using dietary supplements, such as vitamins, or any complementary or alternative medicines or medical practices. Some supplements or herbal remedies can damage the liver.</p></content>
